//: A detached conversation is built as `conversation-<id>` (see `open_conversation_window` in lib.rs). Listing only `main` here granted it no window permissions at all, so its traffic lights did nothing and its title bar could not drag the window -- the frontend called `startDragging`, `minimize` and `close`, and Tauri rejected every one because the capability did not cover that label. Decorations are off on both kinds of window, so the app *is* the title bar; without these the second window had no way to be moved, resized or closed.
//http: Outbound HTTP for the harness client, and nothing else. The harness serves no CORS headers -- a sweep of `STUDIO HARNESS/src/` for `cors` and `Access-Control` finds none -- and the webview's origin is `http://tauri.localhost`, which is cross-origin to a loopback port, so every browser fetch died at the preflight. Adding CORS to the harness was the wrong fix: a loopback service holding provider credentials should not be reachable by any origin a browser will preflight, and an allow-list is a config value that gets widened to `*` during a debugging session and never narrowed. Issuing the request from Rust removes the origin and the preflight entirely. The `http:default` set is the five fetch commands (fetch, fetch-send, fetch-read-body, fetch-cancel, fetch-cancel-body) and, per its own description, NO origins at all -- it is inert until a scope is attached, which is what the `allow` list above is. All five commands are genuinely used: the JS wrapper calls fetch and fetch_send on the way out, fetch_read_body on the way back, and fetch_cancel/fetch_cancel_body when an AbortSignal fires, which is how the client's request timeout works. Scope entries are URL patterns (see `HttpScopeEntry` in gen/schemas/acl-manifests.json). Two entries rather than one because hostname matching is literal, not resolved: the plugin's own test suite asserts `http://local:8080` is refused by a `http://localhost:8080` entry, so `127.0.0.1` does not cover `localhost` or the reverse. Both are admitted because either may appear in VITE_HARNESS_BASE_URL, and the CSP `connect-src` already admits both. The port is the only wildcard, because the harness binds an ephemeral port chosen at launch. The path is wildcarded implicitly: `parse_url_pattern` in the plugin's scope.rs rewrites an empty pathname to `*`, and leaves scheme and hostname exact -- its tests assert `https://localhost:8080` is refused by an `http://localhost:8080` entry. So this grant is scheme-exact, host-exact, port-any, path-any, and reaches nothing off this machine. No `https://**`, no host wildcard, no IPv6 `[::1]` entry -- the harness reports `127.0.0.1` in its readiness frame and binds it explicitly, so a v6 entry would be scope nobody asked for.
//store: FE-02. This was `store:default`, which the generated ACL manifest expands to all fourteen store operations (load, get-store, set, get, has, delete, clear, reset, keys, values, entries, length, reload, save) on any file the webview names. The appearance feature calls exactly five of them against exactly one file: `load` opens `preferences.json`, then `get`, `set`, `delete`, `save` (src/design/theme/appearance.ts:58, 76, 83/97, 119, 84/98/120). Those five are what is granted now. A path scope was wanted here too and is not available: tauri-plugin-store 2.4.4 declares `global_scope_schema: null` in gen/schemas/acl-manifests.json, so the plugin defines no scope vocabulary and there is nothing to pin `preferences.json` with. The file therefore remains reachable by name only, and the standing rule stands on its own: this store is plaintext JSON in the app config dir and no credential ever enters it.
